claim: Arctic regions have experienced strong warming over recent decades.
source: Arctic regions have experienced strong warming over recent decades (Box et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Box et al., 2019

claim: Mean July temperatures in the Arctic region could be less than +2°C warmer by the end of the 21st century under RCP 2.6.
source: Following climate simulations, mean July temperatures in the region could be, by the end of the 21st century, less than +2°C warmer with ambitious mitigation efforts (RCP 2.6), about +3.1°C (intermediate effort scenario RCP 4.5), or an extreme of +14°C warmer (high-emission high-warming RCP 8.5).
evidence: Based on climate simulations with RCP scenarios from Meinshausen et al., 2011

claim: Mean July temperatures in the Arctic region could be about +3.1°C warmer by the end of the 21st century under RCP 4.5.
source: Following climate simulations, mean July temperatures in the region could be, by the end of the 21st century, less than +2°C warmer with ambitious mitigation efforts (RCP 2.6), about +3.1°C (intermediate effort scenario RCP 4.5), or an extreme of +14°C warmer (high-emission high-warming RCP 8.5).
evidence: Based on climate simulations with RCP scenarios from Meinshausen et al., 2011

claim: Mean July temperatures in the Arctic region could be +14°C warmer by the end of the 21st century under RCP 8.5.
source: Following climate simulations, mean July temperatures in the region could be, by the end of the 21st century, less than +2°C warmer with ambitious mitigation efforts (RCP 2.6), about +3.1°C (intermediate effort scenario RCP 4.5), or an extreme of +14°C warmer (high-emission high-warming RCP 8.5).
evidence: Based on climate simulations with RCP scenarios from Meinshausen et al., 2011

claim: The treeline ecotone can expand and will squeeze Arctic regions from the south with limited refugial potential in the north.
source: In consequence, the treeline ecotone can expand and will squeeze Arctic regions from the south and have only limited refugial potential in the north (Hofgaard et al., 2012; MacDonald et al., 2007) as simulation studies predicted (Rupp et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hofgaard et al., 2012; MacDonald et al., 2007; and Rupp et al., 2001

claim: Siberian tundra areas are known for their high regional floristic diversity and species biodiversity.
source: The Siberian tundra areas are known for their high regional floristic diversity and species biodiversity (Pauli et al., 2012; Mod and Luoto, 2016; Arctic Climate Impact Assessment, 2004; Schmidt et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Pauli et al., 2012; Mod and Luoto, 2016; Arctic Climate Impact Assessment, 2004; Schmidt et al., 2017

claim: In Siberia, the treeline is formed solely by larch species growing on permafrost.
source: This and the fact that in Siberia the treeline is formed solely by larch species growing on permafrost while in North America this niche is covered by a mix of species (Mamet et al., 2019; Herzschuh and Jordan, 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to Mamet et al., 2019; Herzschuh and Jordan, 2019

claim: In North America, the treeline niche is covered by a mix of species.
source: This and the fact that in Siberia the treeline is formed solely by larch species growing on permafrost while in North America this niche is covered by a mix of species (Mamet et al., 2019; Herzschuh and Jordan, 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to Mamet et al., 2019; Herzschuh and Jordan, 2019

claim: Empirical studies show slower treeline responses than equilibrium-based estimations, with either no treeline advance or rates of only a few metres per year in Siberia.
source: Equilibrium-based estimations are not backed by empirical studies which are showing slower responses and either no treeline advance or rates of only a few metres per year in Siberia (Scherrer et al., 2020; Kharuk et al., 2018; Wieczorek et al., 2017b; Rees et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple empirical studies: Scherrer et al., 2020; Kharuk et al., 2018; Wieczorek et al., 2017b; Rees et al., 2020

claim: LAVESI is an individual-based spatially explicit vegetation model developed for the northern Siberian treeline ecotone.
source: For the northern Siberian treeline ecotone, the vegetation model LAVESI was developed, which incorporates a full tree (Larix) life cycle beginning with seed production and dispersal, germination, and establishment of seedlings, which then grow based on abiotic (temperature, precipitation, active-layer depth) and biotic (competition) conditions (Kruse et al., 2019a, Kruse et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kruse et al., 2019a, Kruse et al., 2016

claim: LAVESI can capture the nonlinear response of treeline populations well at a regional level on the Taimyr Peninsula.
source: Although soil nutrients and mycorrhiza are not considered explicitly in the current version, it was shown that it can capture the nonlinear response of the treeline populations well at a regional level on the Taimyr Peninsula (Kruse et al., 2019a, Kruse et al., 2016; Wieczorek et al., 2017b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kruse et al., 2019a, Kruse et al., 2016; Wieczorek et al., 2017b

claim: The treeline follows climate warming with a severe, century-long time lag.
source: Our simulations reveal that the treeline follows climate warming with a severe, century-long time lag, which is overcompensated by infilling of stands in the long run even when temperatures cool again.
evidence: Based on simulation results from the LAVESI model presented in this study

claim: Under RCP 2.6, approximately 30% of original tundra areas will remain in the north but separated into two disjunct refugia.
source: Our simulations reveal that only under ambitious mitigation strategies (relative concentration pathway 2.6) will ∼30% of original tundra areas remain in the north but separated into two disjunct refugia.
evidence: Based on simulation results from the LAVESI model presented in this study

claim: The treeline reaches a severe migration lag of hundreds of years when relating its position to the climate-analogue.
source: When relating and tracking the position of the treeline to the climate (=climate-analogue), we find a severe migration lag of hundreds of years until simulations reach the same position (Figure 2).
evidence: Based on simulation results shown in Figure 2

claim: Simulated treeline migration rates over the past few decades are generally in line with modern observations showing only a slow treeline advance.
source: Regardless, our simulated rates over the past few decades are generally in line with the few existing modern observations showing only a slow treeline advance (Mamet et al., 2019; Hansson et al., 2021; Rees et al., 2020; Shevtsova et al., 2020; Guo and Rees, 2020).
evidence: Comparison of simulation results with cited observational studies

claim: Migration rates are especially high in Chukotka in all forcing scenarios.
source: Rates are especially high in Chukotka, however, in all forcing scenarios (Appendix 2—table 1): an observation that can be attributed to forest patches ahead of the current treeline, which serve as nuclei for tundra infilling (shown by, e.g. Snell and Cowling, 2015; Kharuk et al., 2018; Kruse et al., 2019a; Harsch and Bader, 2011).
evidence: Based on simulation results in Appendix 2—table 1 and supported by citations

claim: Forest patches ahead of the current treeline serve as nuclei for tundra infilling.
source: Rates are especially high in Chukotka, however, in all forcing scenarios (Appendix 2—table 1): an observation that can be attributed to forest patches ahead of the current treeline, which serve as nuclei for tundra infilling (shown by, e.g. Snell and Cowling, 2015; Kharuk et al., 2018; Kruse et al., 2019a; Harsch and Bader, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Snell and Cowling, 2015; Kharuk et al., 2018; Kruse et al., 2019a; Harsch and Bader, 2011

claim: The simulated migration rates are high compared to those during post-glacial migration.
source: Generally, the simulated rates are high compared to those during post-glacial migration (e.g. Feurdean et al., 2013) but seem likely as future climate is unprecedented, especially in their rate of change.
evidence: Comparison with cited post-glacial migration rates from Feurdean et al., 2013

claim: The treeline reaches more advanced positions than the climate analogue after the initial migration lag.
source: After the initial migration lag, we can see from our millennium-long simulations that the treeline reaches more advanced positions than the climate analogue (Figure 2, Appendix 2—table 1, Appendix 2—figure 1, Appendix 2—figure 2, Appendix 3—figure 1).
evidence: Based on simulation results shown in multiple figures

claim: Strong overshooting occurs in scenarios with cooling temperatures back to the 20th-century level.
source: This strong overshooting was unexpected especially in scenarios with cooling temperatures back to the 20th-century level.
evidence: Based on simulation results from this study

claim: Once established, trees can endure periods of unfavourable environments.
source: However, we designed our model to be pattern-oriented and is based on observations that, once established, trees can endure periods of unfavourable environments (compare Kruse et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kruse et al., 2016

claim: Trees ahead of the treeline act as nuclei for tundra colonization when conditions improve.
source: This leads to the survival of trees ahead of the treeline acting as nuclei for tundra colonization when conditions improve (Väliranta et al., 2011; Snell and Cowling, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Väliranta et al., 2011; Snell and Cowling, 2015

claim: Elevational treelines retreat slower than expected because trees can persist until dramatic events cause the death of all well-established trees.
source: This is backed by observations of slower-than-expected retreat of elevational treelines because trees can persist until dramatic events cause the death of all well-established trees (Scherrer et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Scherrer et al., 2020

claim: The area loss over time roughly follows a negative exponential function, which is steeper the warmer the climate scenarios are.
source: The area loss over time roughly follows a negative exponential function, which is steeper the warmer the climate scenarios are (Figure 3, Appendix 3—figure 1).
evidence: Based on simulation results shown in Figure 3 and Appendix 3—figure 1

claim: Under RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5, the quickest tundra loss occurs by approximately 2100 CE.
source: The quickest loss, already by ∼2100 CE, is seen in the intermediate warming scenario RCP 4.5 (+3°C July temperatures) and the extreme RCP 8.5 (July temperatures +14°C).
evidence: Based on simulation results from this study

claim: Under RCP 4.5 and RCP 8.5, tundra retreats to its minimum cover of 5.7% by the middle of the millennium.
source: For these scenarios, tundra retreats to its minimum cover of 5.7% by the middle of the millennium (lower panels in Figure 3).
evidence: Based on simulation results shown in Figure 3

claim: Under mitigation scenario RCP 2.6, the tundra area is reduced to 32.7%.
source: Even under mitigation scenario RCP 2.6, the tundra area is reduced to 32.7% or in the very ambitious scenario 2.6* to only 54.9%.
evidence: Based on simulation results from this study

claim: Under scenario RCP 2.6*, the tundra area is reduced to 54.9%.
source: Even under mitigation scenario RCP 2.6, the tundra area is reduced to 32.7% or in the very ambitious scenario 2.6* to only 54.9%.
evidence: Based on simulation results from this study

claim: Cooling back to 20th century levels led to a slight tundra re-expansion of a few percent of the area by the end of the simulations.
source: Cooling back to the 20th century levels led to a slight tundra re-expansion of a few percent of the area by the end of the simulations.
evidence: Based on simulation results from this study

claim: Only if humans act ambitiously in limiting global warming to well below +2°C (RCP 2.6, 2.6*), and temperatures actually cool after the maximum, approximately 10–30% of the tundra area could persist in the north and can re-expand after the mid-millennium maximum treeline extent.
source: In consequence, only if humans act ambitiously in limiting global warming to well below +2°C (RCP 2.6, 2.6*), and temperatures actually cool after the maximum, do simulations show that ∼10–30% of the tundra area could persist in the north and can re-expand after the mid-millennium maximum treeline extent.
evidence: Based on simulation results from this study

claim: Due to the overshooting effect, less than 10% of the tundra area remains unforested.
source: However, due to the overshooting effect, less than 10% of the area remains unforested.
evidence: Based on simulation results from this study

claim: Tundra is reduced to approximately 5.7% of its current area at maximum forest expansion under the most likely scenario RCP 4.5 after an initial migration lag.
source: Following our simulation results, tundra is reduced to ∼5.7% of its current area at maximum forest expansion under the most likely scenario RCP 4.5 after an initial migration lag.
evidence: Based on simulation results from this study

claim: Only ambitious strategies to mitigate climate warming (e.g. RCP 2.6) could prevent extensive tundra loss and retain approximately 32.7% of the current tundra.
source: Only ambitious strategies to mitigate climate warming (e.g. RCP 2.6) could prevent such an extensive loss and retain ∼32.7% of the current tundra.
evidence: Based on simulation results from this study

claim: The northern refugia are located in Chukotka and the Taimyr Peninsula, currently covered by High Arctic and Arctic tundra types which have relatively high biodiversity.
source: In both cases, the northern refugia are located in Chukotka and the Taimyr Peninsula, currently covered by High Arctic and Arctic tundra types which have relatively high biodiversity (Arctic Climate Impact Assessment, 2004).
evidence: Based on simulation results and supported by citation to Arctic Climate Impact Assessment, 2004

claim: The current total cover of protected northern areas is insufficient to achieve the requisite 30% protection necessary for biodiversity conservation.
source: A WWF report (Krever et al., 2009) finds that the current total cover of protected northern areas is insufficient to achieve the requisite 30% protection necessary for biodiversity conservation (Secretariat of the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity, 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Krever et al., 2009 and Secretariat of the United Nations Convention on Biological Diversity, 2021

claim: Cold-climate tundra types on Siberian islands and in Chukotka are underprotected.
source: Especially cold-climate tundra types on Siberian islands and in Chukotka are underprotected (e.g. Pearson et al., 2013; Walker et al., 2005) and thus further protected areas need to be established.
evidence: Supported by citations to Pearson et al., 2013; Walker et al., 2005

claim: LAVESI handles each tree individually and incorporates a full tree life cycle beginning with seed production and dispersal, germination, and establishment of seedlings.
source: The model LAVESI is an individual-based and spatially explicit model that was developed to study the treeline ecotone growing on permafrost soils on the Taimyr Peninsula (Kruse et al., 2016; Wieczorek et al., 2017b; Epp et al., 2018) and since then it has been improved and modified for different purposes including for migration rate studies (Kruse et al., 2019a). To achieve the most realistic model, each life history stage of the larch individuals is handled explicitly, and the model's processes adapted to observed patterns of surveyed tree stands for the dominant larch tree species, Larix gmelinii and Larix sibirica.
evidence: Supported by citations to Kruse et al., 2016; Wieczorek et al., 2017b; Epp et al., 2018; Kruse et al., 2019a

claim: Warmth, especially summer mean temperatures, cumulative temperatures, and the vegetation period length, are key climate variables for tree establishment and growth.
source: Warmth, especially summer mean temperatures, cumulative temperatures, and the vegetation period length, are key climate variables (e.g. MacDonald et al., 2007) and are hence included in the model for estimating potential tree growth and tree mortality (Kruse et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to MacDonald et al., 2007 and Kruse et al., 2016

claim: Permafrost soils with a shallow active-layer depth limit the space available for rooting and nutrient stores.
source: For example, permafrost soils with a shallow active-layer depth limit the space available for rooting and nutrient stores (e.g. Sullivan et al., 2015) and frozen/cold soils prevent growth but water can support growth in dry summers (Sugimoto et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sullivan et al., 2015 and Sugimoto et al., 2002

claim: Frozen/cold soils prevent growth but water can support growth in dry summers.
source: For example, permafrost soils with a shallow active-layer depth limit the space available for rooting and nutrient stores (e.g. Sullivan et al., 2015) and frozen/cold soils prevent growth but water can support growth in dry summers (Sugimoto et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sugimoto et al., 2002

claim: Even in northernmost areas on the Taimyr Peninsula, mycorrhiza are present even before the invasion of trees in the Holocene.
source: Further limitations could arise from the lack of a suitable mycorrhiza symbiosis partner, but as shown by Hippel et al., 2021 even in northernmost areas on the Taimyr Peninsula mycorrhiza are present even before the invasion of trees in the Holocene.
evidence: Supported by citation to Hippel et al., 2021

claim: Dispersal rates of mycorrhiza with small spores are a magnitude faster than for taxa with larger seeds.
source: Additionally, dispersal rates of mycorrhiza with small spores are a magnitude faster than for taxa with larger seeds so that geographic distance is unlikely to be a limiting factor, similar to diatoms as shown by Stoof-Leichsenring et al., 2015.
evidence: Supported by citation to Stoof-Leichsenring et al., 2015 for diatoms as an analogy

claim: July temperatures increase by a median of +1.2°C (RCP 2.6*), +1.8°C (2.6), +2.1°C (4.5), and up to +5°C (8.5) compared to 1970–2000 until 2100.
source: July temperatures (Figure 1), which have the strongest impact in the model due to a positive influence on tree diameter growth, increase in these scenarios by a median of +1.2°C (RCP 2.6*), +1.8°C (2.6), +2.1°C (4.5), and up to +5°C (8.5) compared to 1970–2000 until 2100
evidence: Based on climate forcing data shown in Figure 1

claim: July temperatures partly cool until 2300 to +0.6°C (RCP 2.6*), +0.5°C (2.6), and reach higher levels for the two warmest scenarios to +3.1°C (4.5) and up to +14°C (8.5).
source: which partly cools until 2300 to +0.6°C (RCP 2.6*), +0.5°C (2.6), and reaches higher levels for the two warmest scenarios to +3.1°C (4.5) and up to +144°C (8.5).
evidence: Based on climate forcing data used in the study

claim: Future climate changes will lead to an increase in extreme weather events.
source: Future climate changes will lead to an increase in extreme weather events (Masson-Delmotte et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to Masson-Delmotte et al., 2021

claim: A higher ignition probability and thus wildfires are expected in the future, to which Siberian boreal forests are sensitive.
source: Future climate changes will lead to an increase in extreme weather events (Masson-Delmotte et al., 2021), among others a higher ignition probability and thus wildfires are expected to which the Siberian boreal forests are sensitive (e.g. Shvidenko and Schepaschenko, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Masson-Delmotte et al., 2021 and Shvidenko and Schepaschenko, 2014

claim: Increases in extreme rainfall events will lead to local flooding and waterlogging.
source: Increases in extreme rainfall events will lead to local flooding and waterlogging (Masson-Delmotte et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citation to Masson-Delmotte et al., 2021

claim: The larch species L. gmelinii dominates the areas to the west of the Verkhoyansk Mountain Range approximately 90–130° E.
source: The larch species L. gmelinii (Rupr.) Rupr. dominates the areas to the west of the Verkhoyansk Mountain Range ∼90–130° E and its sister species L. cajanderi Mill. grows in northeast Siberia Figure 1 (Abaimov, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Abaimov, 2010

claim: The larch species L. cajanderi grows in northeast Siberia.
source: The larch species L. gmelinii (Rupr.) Rupr. dominates the areas to the west of the Verkhoyansk Mountain Range ∼90–130° E and its sister species L. cajanderi Mill. grows in northeast Siberia Figure 1 (Abaimov, 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Abaimov, 2010

claim: The decrease of the albedo when tundra is colonized by tree stands leads to a positive feedback with climate.
source: Therefore, the expected decrease of the albedo leading to a positive feedback with climate when tundra is colonized by tree stands (e.g. Pearson et al., 2013) is neglected here.
evidence: Supported by citation to Pearson et al., 2013

claim: Considering albedo feedback would likely further increase the rate of transition from tundra to forests.
source: Considering this would likely further increase the rate of transition from tundra to forests.
evidence: Logical inference from the positive feedback mechanism

claim: The model used for this study is solely forced by climate data and no vegetation feedback on permafrost soils and climate was implemented.
source: The model used for this study is solely forced by climate data and no vegetation feedback on permafrost soils and climate was implemented.
evidence: Description of model limitations

claim: LAVESI can be a tool to assess population genetics and aid in the optimal placement of migration corridors and areas to protect.
source: Due to its individual-based nature, LAVESI can be a tool to assess population genetics and aid in the optimal placement of migration corridors and areas to protect (cf. Zurell et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zurell et al., 2021

claim: The diversity in the approximately 2500 km distant refugia fragments is threatened by the fundamental disadvantages of a small population (inbreeding/genetic drift).
source: Although the large refugia could enable tundra species survival and later recolonization (analogon forests, Harsch et al., 2009; Clark, 1998; Stralberg et al., 2020), the diversity in these ~2500 km distant fragments is threatened by the fundamental disadvantages of a small population (inbreeding/genetic drift, Ohsawa and Ide, 2008; Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 1987; Mona et al., 2014; May et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ohsawa and Ide, 2008; Charlesworth and Charlesworth, 1987; Mona et al., 2014; May et al., 2013

claim: Large refugia could enable tundra species survival and later recolonization.
source: Although the large refugia could enable tundra species survival and later recolonization (analogon forests, Harsch et al., 2009; Clark, 1998; Stralberg et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Harsch et al., 2009; Clark, 1998; Stralberg et al., 2020

claim: A network of connected systems would be necessary with protection of potential refugia distributed across the approximately 4000-km-wide tundra area.
source: A network of connected systems would be necessary with protection of potential refugia (e.g. Morelli et al., 2020) distributed across the ~4000-km-wide tundra area.
evidence: Supported by citation to Morelli et al., 2020

claim: The expansion of forests in response to increasing temperature threatens the existence of various types of sensitive tundra.
source: This turnover threatens the existence of various types of sensitive tundra with differing vegetation structure along latitudinal and elevational bioclimatic gradients located between the treeline in the south and the Arctic Ocean in the north (Walker et al., 2005; Pearson et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Walker et al., 2005; Pearson et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2009

claim: Tundra supports special (indigenous) types of land use (e.g. reindeer herding, foraging).
source: The Siberian tundra areas are known for their high regional floristic diversity and species biodiversity (Pauli et al., 2012; Mod and Luoto, 2016; Arctic Climate Impact Assessment, 2004; Schmidt et al., 2017) and support special (indigenous) types of land use (e.g. reindeer herding, foraging).
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: The timing of future tundra loss is uncertain and challenging conservation efforts.
source: However, the expansion of forests in response to increasing temperature is not well understood and the uncertain timing of future tundra loss is challenging conservation efforts.
evidence: Stated as a knowledge gap

claim: Models that do not consider small-scale processes lead to forecasts prone to overestimating treeline advance.
source: Models that do not consider these processes lead to forecasts prone to overestimating treeline advance (compare Pearson et al., 2013; Snell and Cowling, 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Pearson et al., 2013; Snell and Cowling, 2015

claim: Other simulation studies show 50% tundra loss during the 21st century.
source: Other simulation studies show 50% loss during the 21st century (Callaghan et al., 2005; Kaplan et al., 2003; Pearson et al., 2013) but not the dynamics of the long run until the end of 3000 CE, as shown by our study.
evidence: Supported by citations to Callaghan et al., 2005; Kaplan et al., 2003; Pearson et al., 2013

claim: The expansion of forests will likely put especially cold-climate tundra types at risk of extinction.
source: All in all, the expansion is in accordance with other studies and will likely put especially cold-climate tundra types at risk of extinction (e.g. Pearson et al., 2013; Walker et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pearson et al., 2013; Walker et al., 2005

claim: Permafrost degradation/abrupt thaw and warming could lead to thermokarst processes that would locally cause swamping/waterlogging, leading to suppressed establishment/growth.
source: Permafrost degradation/abrupt thaw and warming (Biskaborn et al., 2019; Stuenzi et al., 2021) could lead to thermokarst processes that would locally cause swamping/waterlogging, leading to suppressed establishment/growth (Rees et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Biskaborn et al., 2019; Stuenzi et al., 2021; Rees et al., 2020

claim: Thermokarst processes are unlikely to limit tree invasion on a broader scale.
source: which is not explicitly simulated and unlikely to limit tree invasion on a broader scale.
evidence: Author's inference based on the model design

claim: Interspecific competition of recruits with present shrubs or grasses which are increasing more quickly is called the greening of the Arctic.
source: On the other hand, interspecific competition of recruits with present shrubs or grasses which are increasing more quickly – called the greening of the Arctic (Pearson et al., 2013; Berner et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Pearson et al., 2013; Berner et al., 2020

claim: Herbivory by browsers reduces the survival and growth rate by damaging the shoots.
source: Further biotic interactions are implicitly included, such as herbivory by browsers (e.g. Wielgolaski et al., 2017), which reduces the survival and growth rate by damaging the shoots (compare krummholz study by Kruse et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citations to Wielgolaski et al., 2017 and Kruse et al., 2020

claim: Herbivory can lead to a snow compaction cooling effect on soil temperatures.
source: and can lead to a snow compaction cooling effect on soil temperatures (Beer et al., 2020)
evidence: Supported by citation to Beer et al., 2020

claim: Pest outbreaks are likely to increase in the future.
source: or pest outbreaks that are likely to increase in the future (e.g. larch silk moth, Fedotova et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fedotova et al., 2019

claim: Considering additional limiting factors would most likely lead to a further reduction of migration rates.
source: This would most likely lead to a further reduction of migration rates.
evidence: Logical inference from the discussion of limiting factors

claim: In a hotter environment, fires could lead to dramatic forest losses and areas might be turned into steppe and not revert to the prior tundra.
source: Fire is not yet explicitly simulated in the model and in a hotter environment fires could lead to dramatic forest losses. Areas might be turned into steppe and not revert to the prior tundra.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about fire effects not included in the model

claim: Tundra colonization would most likely be slowed down in the lowlands but less so in the well-drained mountainous regions due to waterlogging effects.
source: The anticipated effect to the LAVESI predictions is that tundra colonization would most likely be slowed down in the lowlands but less so in the well-drained mountainous regions, which would further prolong the time-lagged response of the treeline migration.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about effects not explicitly modeled

claim: The migration lag behavior is longer than expected from the properties of treeline-forming larch species with generation times of decades and weak long-distance dispersal rates.
source: This behaviour is longer than expected from the properties of treeline-forming larch species with generation times of decades and weak long-distance dispersal rates (e.g. Mamet et al., 2019; Kruse et al., 2019a; Scherrer et al., 2020; Clark, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mamet et al., 2019; Kruse et al., 2019a; Scherrer et al., 2020; Clark, 1998

claim: Other processes not yet explicitly captured by the model may constrain the migration process, such as the strong greening of the Arctic increasing interspecific competition, the warming and abrupt thaw of permafrost, soil nutrients, and animal activity.
source: Other processes, not yet explicitly captured by the model, may constrain the migration process, such as the strong greening of the Arctic increasing interspecific competition (compare Pearson et al., 2013; Berner et al., 2020), the warming and abrupt thaw of permafrost (e.g. Stuenzi et al., 2021; Biskaborn et al., 2019), soil nutrients (e.g. Sullivan et al., 2015), and animal activity (e.g. Wielgolaski et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to Pearson et al., 2013; Berner et al., 2020; Stuenzi et al., 2021; Biskaborn et al., 2019; Sullivan et al., 2015; Wielgolaski et al., 2017
